summary: This report summarizes the POISED working group, covering the events that led to its formation and its work through the end of 1992. POISED looked at how the IETF should organize its own processes. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A group was formed to figure out how the Internet standards club should run itself. This paper tells the story of why the group started and what it did in its first stretch.

questions: what was the poised working group
how are iab and iesg members selected
subtitle: How a 1992 working group reworked the way IETF and IAB leaders are chosen and how standards decisions are made.

tldr.problem: After a clash over IP evolution in 1992, the Internet community questioned who makes decisions and how the IESG and IAB are populated.
tldr.mechanism: The POISED working group debated for months, converged at the November 1992 IETF on the IESG making all standards-track decisions, and defined a nomination committee with set terms and a recall process.
tldr.outcome: A new selection process was to start by the March IETF meeting, with a new charter for the IAB and IETF still to be drafted. This memo is informational.

today: RFC 1396 is an Informational report covering events through the end of 1992, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It records a moment in how the IETF, IAB and IESG were organized, not a current process description.

sections.title: How POISED Began
sections.content:
The POISED working group grew from two strands of activity. In 1991 there was concern that the IP address space was running out and routing tables were growing too large; the ROAD Working Group studied this and made a short-term recommendation but no long-term plan. In June 1992 the IAB considered the IESG's follow-up plan and raised ideas from the CLNP protocol, which caused controversy both technical and political: who makes decisions, and who chooses the deciders?

The author says miscommunication played a part: many read an IAB memo as a decision when the IAB meant it as advice, and the creation of the IESG and area directorates had put two or three layers between a working group and the IAB. After the July IETF meeting, Internet Society president Vint Cerf asked for a working group, which was formed in August with Steve Crocker as chair.
sections.plainLanguage: People argued about how to change the Internet and about who gets to decide. So a group was formed to fix the deciding part.

sections.title: Deliberations and the November IETF
sections.content:
From August to mid-November an estimated 20 MB of messages circulated. The main point was the need for a well defined process for selecting leaders with community representation. Carl Malamud and Steve Crocker then proposed replacing the IAB and IESG with two boards, one for technical management and one for process oversight, with defined terms and selection by committees.

At the November IETF in Washington D.C., IAB and IESG members proposed changes inside the existing structure that matched the process elements of that proposal. The key point was that all processing of standards actions, including the final decision to advance a specification, would be made by the IESG. This shortened the decision cycle and made a radical restructuring unnecessary. Afterwards the IAB cleared its queue and the IESG began handling standards actions itself.
sections.plainLanguage: First someone suggested tearing everything down and starting over. Then the existing leaders agreed to a smaller change that fixed the main problem, so nobody had to start over.

sections.title: Selecting and Recalling Leaders
sections.content:
The IETF has no formal membership and decides by consensus rather than by vote, so formal voting was set aside. Instead IAB and IESG members are chosen by a nomination and recruiting committee of seven community volunteers (chosen by lot if more volunteer), plus non-voting representatives of the IAB and IESG and a non-voting chair from the ISOC. Volunteers must have attended two IETF meetings.

Members serve two years, with half of each body starting in odd years and half in even years. IESG selections are ratified by the IAB, and IAB selections by the ISOC. If the committee cannot agree on one candidate it may forward several to the ratifying body.

For recall, the ISOC supplies an ombudsman to field complaints once other oversight is exhausted. If the matter is unresolved after a cooling-off period, a randomly chosen recall committee of volunteers considers it, and a two thirds vote is needed to remove someone.
sections.plainLanguage: Leaders are picked by a small group of volunteers drawn like raffle tickets, serve for two years, and can be removed if a fair panel agrees by a big enough majority.

sections.title: ISOC Approval and Next Steps
sections.content:
On December 10 and 11 the Internet Society Trustees met in Reston, VA. Crocker asked them, on behalf of the IETF, to approve the general direction and to give temporary approval to the selection process so the first round could proceed. The Trustees were strongly approving of the work, but raised concern about the ISOC's legal liability for IESG decisions and said they did not intend to micromanage the IETF.

The memo ends with the plan to run the first selection in January and February, ideally finished by the end of February and before the next IETF meeting, with new members starting their terms at the end of the March meeting. A new charter for the IAB and IETF, to be adopted by the ISOC, was the next item for the working group.
sections.plainLanguage: The people who oversee the whole group said yes to the plan for now, and the next job was to write down the official rules.

sections.title: The Charter and Cerf's Request
sections.content:
The memo attaches Vint Cerf's request of 12 August 1992 and the working group charter. Cerf named three topics: procedures for appointments to the IAB, for resolving disagreements among the IETF, IESG and IAB, and for confirming that standards procedures were followed so everyone had a fair chance to be heard. He pointed to RFC 1358 for the IAB charter and RFC 1310 for the standards process.

The charter set milestones from September to December 1992 and required the mailing list and all discussions to be completely open. It targeted a final report as an Informational RFC for the ISOC Board meeting in December 1992.
sections.plainLanguage: The papers at the end show the original request to form the group and the list of jobs it was given, all done in the open.
